sweep_summary: Bulgarian (bulg1262) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Leafgren 2011. The four title-keyword items split as follows. (1) Dimitrova et al. 2018 (Speech Prosody) downloaded open from the ISCA archive and read in full: an age-variation study of intonation, phrasing and pauses; silent on word-stress placement, priority none. (2) Franks 2008 (JSL 16) is about clitic-cluster placement and its prosody, not lexical stress; Project MUSE paywall, no OA copy anywhere (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/S2/CORE/JSL OJS archive checked); low priority. (3) Bidwell 1968 (Studies in Linguistics 20:41-47) is a dedicated noun-stress study but print-only: archive.org's microfilm run lacks vol. 20 and HathiTrust was bot-blocked; medium priority as it would refine the lexical coding with noun pattern classes. (4) Grigorjan 1976 (Zeitschrift fur Slawistik 21:738-741, German) treats words with double/variable stress in the literary language - a refinement within a lexical system; De Gruyter paywalled, low priority. No works with stress in the title contradicts the catalog. The best first-hand statement read is Patseva ROA-1612 p. 5 ('defined traditionally as free.. cannot be inferred directly by the phonetic and morphological structure of the word'), confirming 'lexical'; it and Ternes & Vladimirova-Buhtz 1990 (minimal pair para 'steam' / para 'coin') were already held by the project from the compilation of 9/16 and do not supersede Leafgren.org, ISCA and search-engine HTML (mostly blocked or off-target).

new_statements.quote: Bulgarian accent has been defined traditionally as free. The place of the word stress has been considered a result of historical regularities, which have acted in the past and have been changed. Today, the lexical accent cannot be inferred directly by the phonetic and morphological structure of the word (Tilkov & Bojadžiev 2013: 156). According to the traditional Bulgarian linguistics the word stress can appear on almost any syllable of the word, as well as on various morphological units like prefixes, roots, suffixes and articles.

None of the four works with stress in the title yielded a readable stress-placement statement; this is the best first-hand statement read during this search of works with stress in the title, but it was downloaded on 9/16 and should not be counted as a new find.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's free/lexical stress reading and with Patseva (ROA-1612) and Ternes & Vladimirova-Buhtz (1990): stress is shown to fall on the ending in some verbs and on the stem in others of the same class, with no rule given, and it adds the morphological detail that the imperfect suffix -ях/-ех is chosen by the position of stress. It is an implicit, not an explicit, statement about stress type; confidence for the reading is accordingly low.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given; the book is an intermediate-level thematic workbook with grammar sections on tenses, pronouns and reported speech and has no alphabet or pronunciation section (contents, p. 6). The only mention of stress is morphological: for -Е and -И conjugation verbs the imperfect suffix is -ЯХ when the stress is on the ending (четЕ – четЯХ, спИ – спЯХ) and -ЕХ when it is not (пишЕ – пишЕХ, ходИ – ходЕХ). This presupposes that stress position differs lexically between verbs of the same class (ending-stressed vs stem-stressed) and is not derivable from the conjugation type; the stressed vowel is marked throughout the grammar tables by a capital letter. That is compatible with free lexical stress, but the work states no general rule.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the passage is about verb-suffix allomorphy, not about stress placement itself
new_statements.identity_note: All four listed works concern standard (literary) Bulgarian; none describes a particular dialect. The Peace Corps workbook is a teaching text of the standard language for American volunteers.

tone_statements.quote: The Bulgarian intonational system comprises an inventory of five pitch accents (L*, L*+H, L+H*, H*, H+!H*), two phrase accents (L- and H-) and three boundary tones (L%, H% and %H). … The default pre-nuclear pitch accent is L*+H, and the default nuclear one is H*. … We hypothesize an anchorage domain, namely, the prosodic word, where the L* is aligned with the onset of the lexically stressed syllable (or just before it), while the H trailing tone aligns with a following unstressed syllable within the domain of the prosodic word.

tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone: all pitch events are intonational (pitch accents L*, L*+H, L+H*, H*, H+!H*; phrase accents L-, H-; boundary tones %H, L%, H%), starred tones dock on the lexically stressed syllable.

tone_statements.quote: In agreement with the original model by Pierrehumbert (1980) for English, the tone-bearing unit in Bulgarian is a syllable. … The tonal accent (TA) L*+H primarily associates with the metrically strong rhythmic foot (Σs). This connection runs upwards through the prosodic tree to the head of the foot σs, i .e. to the metrically strong syllable. … the boundary tones and the phrase accents are regarded as products of the peripheral association with the constituent nodes higher in the prosodic hierarchy.

Diese Verbindung verläuft abwärts durch den prosodischen Baum zum Kopf des Fußes σs (der metrisch starken Silbe). … In den Daten aus dem MapTask- und dem gelesenen Korpus wurden die Tonakzente L*, L*+H, L+H*, (!)H*, H*, H+!H*/L*; die Phrasenakzente L- und H- und die Grenztöne L%, H% festgestellt.
tone_statements.translation: The tone-bearing unit in Bulgarian is the syllable, as in Pierrehumbert's (1980) original model for English. … The pitch accent L*+H (TA) is primarily associated with the metrically strong foot (Σs). This link runs down through the prosodic tree to the head of the foot σs (the metrically strong syllable). … In the data from the MapTask and the read corpus the pitch accents L*, L*+H, L+H*, (!)H*, H*, H+!H*/L*, the phrase accents L- and H- and the boundary tones L%, H% were established.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4.1.2 'Der prosodische Baum im Bulgarischen', pp. 93-94 + Kap. 8 Zusammenfassung p. 149 (same inventory sec. 4.3 p. 104)
tone_statements.summary: Pitch in Sofia Bulgarian analysed as purely intonational, as in English: postlexical accents L*, L*+H, L+H*, (!)H*, H*, H+!H* dock on stressed syllables; phrase accents L-, H-; boundary tones L%, H%.
